---
title: "Dead Ends?"
---

Work that didn't reach publication: studies I abandoned, analyses that went
nowhere, and tools I built and stopped using. I keep this page because the
published record makes research look far tidier than it is, and because *how* a
design fails is usually more instructive than how one succeeds.

For each entry I report the idea, what I actually did, who the participants
were, and what was measured — enough that someone could judge whether their own
version would work. **No data is shared here**, and none of these datasets are
mine to distribute.

Nothing on this page is a confession. Most of it is ordinary.

## Abandoned analyses

### Predicting bottom-out behaviour from tutoring logs {#bottom-out}

*Summer 2025 · shelved after modelling*

**The idea.** In an intelligent tutoring system, students can request hints
repeatedly until the system simply gives the answer — "bottoming out." It looks
like help-seeking but often functions as answer-seeking. I wanted to know
whether the *sequence* of a student's interactions predicted bottoming out
before it happened, using recurrent architectures that treat the log as a time
series rather than a bag of counts.

**What I did.** Built the pipeline in R, calling Python through `reticulate`.
Reshaped interaction logs into three-dimensional tensors (student × lag ×
feature) and fitted recurrent neural networks, including LSTMs. Ran
hyperparameter tuning, per-student model fitting on random subsamples of 30 and
100 students, and permutation-based feature-importance analyses to see which
log features carried the signal.

**Participants.** Students represented in an intelligent-tutoring log dataset,
analysed at the level of anonymous learner IDs. **[EDIT: add the grade range,
subject, and N of the full dataset — I could confirm the modelling subsamples
from your scripts but not the sample's demographic composition.]**

**Measures.** Interaction-level log features only — hint requests, attempt
counts, response timing, and item-level correctness — with no self-report or
demographic predictors.

**Why it stopped.** Two reasons, and only one of them is technical. The models
ran, but per-student fitting on a few dozen learners could not distinguish a
genuine sequential signal from overfitting to individual quirks, and I never
resolved how to pool across students without losing the sequence structure that
was the whole point. The other reason is that my role in the project was never
settled, and I stopped before deciding whether it was mine to finish.

**What I'd do differently.** Fix the estimand before the architecture. I chose
the model class first — recurrent networks, because the data were sequential —
and only then asked what quantity I wanted to recover. Reversed, I'd have
noticed earlier that a well-specified multilevel survival model answers the
"when does someone bottom out" question with far less machinery, and would have
been the honest baseline to beat.

### Emotion-dynamics indices without the power to support them

*Paused · analysis-stage dead end*

**The idea.** Test whether within-person emotion dynamics — inertia, variability,
reactivity — carry the mechanism linking a daily stressor to longer-term
adjustment, rather than mean affect doing all the work.

**What I did.** Fitted the dynamic models, derived the person-level dynamic
indices, and carried them into the mechanism models as mediators and moderators.

**Participants and measures.** **[EDIT: fill in N, age range, composition, and
the daily-diary instruments — I deliberately left these blank rather than infer
them from your project notes, since several diary studies in your folder have
different samples and I did not want to publish the wrong numbers.]**

**Why it stopped.** The dynamic indices were too imprecisely estimated at the
person level to support the mechanism test. With around two weeks of daily
reports, an individual's inertia or variability is estimated with enough
uncertainty that treating it as a predictor propagates that noise into every
downstream coefficient. The confidence intervals were consistent with almost
anything of interest. This is a power problem in a specific and underappreciated
sense: not too few people, but too few observations *per* person to treat a
derived dynamic feature as if it were measured.

**What I'd do differently.** Treat the dynamic index as latent rather than
computed — estimate it and its uncertainty inside one model instead of
extracting a point estimate and passing it along. And run the reliability
calculation for person-level dynamic parameters *at design stage*, which would
have told me how many days I needed before any data were collected.

## Tools I built and stopped using

### An automated literature-review pipeline {#auto-lr}

*Version 1.0 · unmaintained*

**The idea.** Screening for a systematic review is mechanical, tedious, and
error-prone in a way that seemed automatable: take exported search results,
fill in the metadata gaps, and triage abstracts against inclusion criteria so a
human only adjudicates the genuinely ambiguous ones.

**What I built.** An R pipeline that ingested CSV exports from LitSift, combined
them across searches, and recovered missing abstracts from the CrossRef API by
DOI, with per-record error handling so one bad response couldn't kill a run. It
worked — abstract coverage improved substantially over the raw exports.

**Participants and measures.** None; the units were published records.

**Why it stopped.** It never got past the easy half. Abstract *retrieval* is a
solved problem; abstract *screening* is the part that matters, and I stalled
exactly there. What I had was a metadata-completion tool wearing the name of a
literature-review tool. It also never had a validation step — I could not have
told you its false-negative rate against my own manual screening, which for a
systematic review is the only number that would justify using it.

**What I'd do differently.** Build the evaluation set first: hand-screen a few
hundred abstracts, then treat any automated screener as something that has to
reproduce those decisions before it is allowed near a real review. That reframes
the project from "write a pipeline" to "measure agreement," which is both more
tractable and more publishable.

### An R package for emotion-regulation dynamics {#er-package}

*Never started*

**The idea.** Package the measures I keep recomputing — dynamic indices,
polyregulation summaries, synchrony estimates — so that I and others could stop
rewriting them per project.

**What I did.** Created the folder in September 2025 and never put anything in
it.

**Why it stopped.** I'm including this because the empty folder is the honest
artifact. The work it was meant to hold does exist, scattered across analysis
scripts in individual projects. What was missing was not time but a decision
about scope: a package needs a settled definition of each measure, and my
definitions were still moving between papers. Packaging a moving target
produces a bad package.

**What I'd do differently.** Wait for the second paper that needs the same
function, then extract it from working code rather than designing it in advance.
